questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Radius of Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
questions.problem: Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3},\,1-t⟩$ at $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{3},\,y(t)=1-t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =3{t}^{2},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =6t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|3{t}^{2}\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 6t|}{{((3t)^{2}+(1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6|t|}{{(9{t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{6|1|}{{(9(1)^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{(10)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =\frac{1}{κ(1)}=\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-1)\,i+(1-t)\,j$ at $t=\frac{1}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{2}-1,\,y(t)=1-t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2t\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 2|}{{((2t)^{2}+(-1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(4{t}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\frac{1}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{2}{{(4{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(1+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{1}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{1}{κ(\frac{1}{2})}=\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)=(1+t)^{2}\,i+(1-t)^{2}\,j$ at $t=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=(1+t)^{2},\,y(t)=(1-t)^{2}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2(1+t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2(1-t) \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2(1+t)\cdot 2-(-2(1-t))\cdot 2|}{{(\,(2(1+t))^{2}+(2(1-t))^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{{(8+8{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{8}{{(8+8(0)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{{(8+0)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the signed curvature of the curve $y=x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ at $x=\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
The signed curvature $k(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
k(x)=\frac{{y}^{″}(x)}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,{y}^{″}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(x) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{[1+{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}k(0) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{{[1+{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-1}{{2}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the signed curvature of the curve $y=x-{e}^{x}$ at $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The signed curvature $k(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
k(x)=\frac{{y}^{″}(x)}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=1-{e}^{x},\,{y}^{″}(x)=-{e}^{x}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(x) & =\frac{-{e}^{x}}{{[1+{(1-{e}^{x})}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{x}}{{(1+1+{e}^{2x}-2{e}^{x})}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{x}}{{(2+{e}^{2x}-2{e}^{x})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}k(1) & =-\frac{{e}^{(1)}}{{(2+{e}^{2(1)}-2{e}^{(1)})}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{e}{({e}^{2}-2e+2)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
